parts.work:
The continuous-time system is
\[
\dot y(t)=a y(t)+u(t), \qquad H(s)=\frac{1}{s-a}.
\]
The given discrete-time approximation is
\[
y[n]=(1+aT_s)y[n-1]+T_s u[n-1].
\]
Rewrite it as
\[
\frac{y[n]-y[n-1]}{T_s}=a y[n-1]+u[n-1].
\]
This is the forward Euler approximation of the derivative:
\[
\dot y(nT_s)\approx \frac{y((n+1)T_s)-y(nT_s)}{T_s},
\]
with the right-hand side evaluated at the previous sample. Equivalently, from the transfer function,
\[
s \approx \frac{z-1}{T_s}.
\]
Thus the discretization method is forward Euler (also called Euler forward difference).

For the continuous-time system,
\[
H(s)=\frac{1}{s-a}.
\]
For the discrete-time system, take the z-transform:
\[
Y(z)=(1+aT_s)z^{-1}Y(z)+T_s z^{-1}U(z),
\]
so
\[
H_d(z)=\frac{Y(z)}{U(z)}
=\frac{T_s z^{-1}}{1-(1+aT_s)z^{-1}}
=\frac{T_s}{z-(1+aT_s)}.
\]
The standard forward Euler substitution is
\[
s=\frac{z-1}{T_s}.
\]
Indeed, substituting this into \(H(s)\) gives
\[
H(s)\bigg|_{s=\frac{z-1}{T_s}}
=\frac{1}{\frac{z-1}{T_s}-a}
=\frac{T_s}{z-1-aT_s}
=\frac{T_s}{z-(1+aT_s)},
\]
which matches \(H_d(z)\). Therefore,
\[
z=1+sT_s.
\]

From part (b),
\[
z=1+sT_s.
\]
Let \(s=\sigma+j\omega\). Then
\[
z=1+T_s(\sigma+j\omega)
=(1+T_s\sigma)+jT_s\omega.
\]
Stable continuous-time poles satisfy
\[
\mathrm{Re}(s)=\sigma<0.
\]
Under the mapping,
\[
\mathrm{Re}(z)=1+T_s\sigma.
\]
Thus \(\sigma<0\) gives
\[
\mathrm{Re}(z)<1.
\]
So the open left half of the \(s\)-plane maps to the open half-plane to the left of the vertical line
\[
\mathrm{Re}(z)=1.
\]
The boundary \(\mathrm{Re}(s)=0\) maps to
\[
z=1+jT_s\omega,
\]
which is the vertical line \(\mathrm{Re}(z)=1\). Since the inequality is strict, the boundary itself is not included. Therefore stable continuous-time poles map into the open region
\[
\{z\in\mathbb C:\mathrm{Re}(z)<1\}.
\]
parts.final:
Stable continuous-time poles with \(\mathrm{Re}(s)<0\) map to the open half-plane
\[
\{z\in\mathbb C:\mathrm{Re}(z)<1\},
\]
i.e. the region strictly to the left of the vertical line \(\mathrm{Re}(z)=1\). The boundary \(\mathrm{Re}(z)=1\) corresponds to \(\mathrm{Re}(s)=0\) and is not included.

parts.work:
The closed-loop system has forward path \(K H(z)\) and unity negative feedback, so its transfer function from \(r\) to \(y\) is
\[
T(z)=\frac{K H(z)}{1+K H(z)}
=\frac{K\frac{b}{1+az^{-1}}}{1+K\frac{b}{1+az^{-1}}}
=\frac{Kb}{1+az^{-1}+Kb}.
\]
With \(K=3\),
\[
T(z)=\frac{3b}{1+3b+a z^{-1}}.
\]
For a constant input \(r_1[n]=1\), the steady-state output is
\[
y_1[\infty]=T(1)\cdot 1=\frac{3b}{1+3b+a}.
\]
Given \(y_1[n]=\frac12\), we get
\[
\frac{3b}{1+3b+a}=\frac12
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
6b=1+3b+a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a=3b-1. \tag{1}
\]

For \(r_2[n]=(-1)^n\), the input has \(z\)-transform corresponding to frequency \(z=-1\). Thus the steady-state output is
\[
y_2[n]=T(-1)(-1)^n.
\]
Now
\[
T(-1)=\frac{3b}{1+3b-a}.
\]
Given \(y_2[n]=\frac32(-1)^n\), we have
\[
\frac{3b}{1+3b-a}=\frac32.
\]
So
\[
6b=3(1+3b-a)=3+9b-3a
\]
\[
0=3+3b-3a
\]
\[
a-b=1. \tag{2}
\]

Solve (1) and (2):
\[
a=3b-1,\qquad a=b+1.
\]
Thus
\[
3b-1=b+1 \Longrightarrow 2b=2 \Longrightarrow b=1.
\]
Then
\[
a=b+1=2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{a=2,\quad b=1}.
\]

With \(b=2\) and \(K=3\), the closed-loop transfer function is
\[
T(z)=\frac{Kb}{1+az^{-1}+Kb}
=\frac{6}{1+6+a z^{-1}}.
\]
Multiply numerator and denominator by \(z\):
\[
T(z)=\frac{6z}{z(1+6)+a}
=\frac{6z}{(7)z+a}.
\]
The closed-loop pole is therefore
\[
z=-\frac{a}{7}.
\]
For BIBO stability of a causal LTI system, all poles must lie strictly inside the unit circle:
\[
\left|-\frac{a}{7}\right|<1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
|a|<7.
\]
Thus the closed-loop system is BIBO stable for
\[
\boxed{-7<a<7}.
\]

We are given
\[
u[n]=a_0+a_1\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right)+a_2(-1)^n.
\]
Write each term as a discrete-time exponential:
\[
\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right)=\frac{e^{j(\pi/2)n}+e^{-j(\pi/2)n}}{2},
\qquad
(-1)^n=e^{j\pi n}.
\]
Thus \(u[n]\) is a sum of components at normalized frequencies
\[
\omega_0=0,\qquad \omega_1=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad \omega_2=\pi,
\]
with corresponding \(z\)-plane locations
\[
z=1,\qquad z=e^{\pm j\pi/2}=\pm j,\qquad z=-1.
\]

We want an LTI filter \(G\) such that
\[
y[n]=a_0+2a_2(-1)^n.
\]
That means:
- the DC component \(a_0\) must pass with gain \(1\);
- the component at \(\omega=\pi/2\) must be completely removed;
- the component at \(\omega=\pi\) must pass with gain \(2\).

So the frequency response must satisfy
\[
H(e^{j0})=1,\qquad H(e^{j\pi/2})=0,\qquad H(e^{-j\pi/2})=0,\qquad H(e^{j\pi})=2.
\]
A causal, stable LTI filter can be designed by placing zeros at \(z=\pm j\) to null the \(\pi/2\) frequency, and choosing the remaining gain to meet the DC and Nyquist specifications.

A simple choice is a second-order FIR filter:
\[
H(z)=K(1-jz^{-1})(1+jz^{-1})=K(1+z^{-2}).
\]
The zeros are at \(z=\pm j\), as required. Now determine \(K\).

At DC, \(z=1\):
\[
H(1)=K(1+1)=2K.
\]
We need \(H(1)=1\), so
\[
2K=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K=\frac12.
\]
Then
\[
H(z)=\frac12(1+z^{-2}).
\]
Check at Nyquist, \(z=-1\):
\[
H(-1)=\frac12(1+1)=1.
\]
But we need gain \(2\) at \(\omega=\pi\). Therefore this filter does not meet the required gain at Nyquist. We need an additional factor that does not disturb the zero at \(z=\pm j\) and can adjust the relative gains at \(z=1\) and \(z=-1\).

Let us use a first-order factor of the form \((1+\alpha z^{-1})\). Then
\[
H(z)=K(1+z^{-2})(1+\alpha z^{-1}).
\]
The zeros at \(z=\pm j\) remain. Now impose the gain conditions.

At \(z=1\):
\[
H(1)=K(2)(1+\alpha)=2K(1+\alpha)=1.
\]
At \(z=-1\):
\[
H(-1)=K(2)(1-\alpha)=2K(1-\alpha)=2.
\]
Divide the second equation by the first:
\[
\frac{2K(1-\alpha)}{2K(1+\alpha)}
=\frac{2}{1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}=2.
\]
Solve:
\[
1-\alpha=2+2\alpha
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
-1=3\alpha
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha=-\frac13.
\]
Then from \(2K(1+\alpha)=1\):
\[
2K\left(1-\frac13\right)=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2K\cdot \frac23=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
K=\frac34.
\]
Thus
\[
H(z)=\frac34(1+z^{-2})\left(1-\frac13 z^{-1}\right).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
H(z)=\frac34\left(1-\frac13 z^{-1}+z^{-2}-\frac13 z^{-3}\right).
\]
So
\[
H(z)=\frac34-\frac14 z^{-1}+\frac34 z^{-2}-\frac14 z^{-3}.
\]

Check:
- At \(z=1\):
\[
H(1)=\frac34(2)\left(\frac23\right)=1.
\]
- At \(z=-1\):
\[
H(-1)=\frac34(2)\left(\frac43\right)=2.
\]
- At \(z=\pm j\): the factor \(1+z^{-2}\) vanishes, so \(H(\pm j)=0\).

Therefore the filter passes DC with gain \(1\), removes \(\pi/2\), and passes Nyquist with gain \(2\). Hence for
\[
u[n]=a_0+a_1\cos(\pi n/2)+a_2(-1)^n,
\]
the output is
\[
y[n]=a_0+2a_2(-1)^n.
\]

Causality: \(H(z)\) is a polynomial in \(z^{-1}\) with no positive powers of \(z\), so the impulse response is causal. Indeed,
\[
h[n]=\frac34\delta[n]-\frac14\delta[n-1]+\frac34\delta[n-2]-\frac14\delta[n-3],
\]
which is zero for \(n<0\).

Stability: The impulse response is finite in length (FIR), hence absolutely summable:
\[
\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|h[n]|<\infty.
\]
Equivalently, all poles are at \(z=0\) (or there are no nonzero poles), so they lie strictly inside the unit circle. Therefore the system is stable.

Final transfer function:
\[
\boxed{H(z)=\frac34\left(1+z^{-2}\right)\left(1-\frac13 z^{-1}\right)
=\frac34-\frac14 z^{-1}+\frac34 z^{-2}-\frac14 z^{-3}}.
\]
parts.final:
\[
H(z)=\frac34\left(1+z^{-2}\right)\left(1-\frac13 z^{-1}\right)
=\frac34-\frac14z^{-1}+\frac34z^{-2}-\frac14z^{-3}.
\]
This is a causal FIR filter, hence causal and stable. It has zeros at \(z=\pm j\), so it removes the \(\cos(\pi n/2)\) term; it has \(H(1)=1\) and \(H(-1)=2\), so it preserves \(a_0\) and doubles the \((-1)^n\) term. Thus \(y[n]=a_0+2a_2(-1)^n\).

parts.work:
The transfer function is
\[
H(z)=0.25(z+2+z^{-1}).
\]
The frequency response is obtained by evaluating \(H(z)\) on the unit circle \(z=e^{j\Omega}\):
\[
H(\Omega)=H(e^{j\Omega})=0.25\left(e^{j\Omega}+2+e^{-j\Omega}\right).
\]
Using \(e^{j\Omega}+e^{-j\Omega}=2\cos\Omega\),
\[
H(\Omega)=0.25(2+2\cos\Omega)=0.5(1+\cos\Omega).
\]
Thus
\[
H(\Omega)=0.5(1+\cos\Omega).
\]
This is real-valued for all \(\Omega\), so the phase is either \(0\) or \(\pi\), depending on the sign of \(H(\Omega)\). Since \(1+\cos\Omega\ge 0\) on \([0,\pi]\), we have \(H(\Omega)\ge 0\). Therefore
\[
|H(\Omega)|=0.5(1+\cos\Omega),\qquad \angle H(\Omega)=0
\]
for \(\Omega\in[0,\pi]\). At \(\Omega=0\), \(H(0)=1\). At \(\Omega=\pi\), \(H(\pi)=0\). The magnitude decreases monotonically from \(1\) to \(0\) over \([0,\pi]\). Equivalently, using \(1+\cos\Omega=2\cos^2(\Omega/2)\),
\[
H(\Omega)=\cos^2(\Omega/2).
\]
So the magnitude is \(\cos^2(\Omega/2)\) and the phase is \(0\) on \([0,\pi]\).
parts.final:
\[
H(\Omega)=0.5(1+\cos\Omega)=\cos^2(\Omega/2).
\]
For \(\Omega\in[0,\pi]\), \(|H(\Omega)|=0.5(1+\cos\Omega)=\cos^2(\Omega/2)\), which decreases monotonically from \(1\) at \(\Omega=0\) to \(0\) at \(\Omega=\pi\). The phase is \(0\) throughout \([0,\pi]\) because \(H(\Omega)\ge 0\).

parts.work:
Write
\[
H(z)=0.25z+0.5+0.25z^{-1}.
\]
The impulse response is the inverse \(z\)-transform:
\[
h[n]=0.25\delta[n+1]+0.5\delta[n]+0.25\delta[n-1].
\]
Thus
\[
h[-1]=0.25,\qquad h[0]=0.5,\qquad h[1]=0.25,
\]
and \(h[n]=0\) otherwise. Since \(h[n]\) has finite duration, the system is FIR. Since \(h[-1]\neq 0\), the system depends on a future input value, so it is non-causal. Equivalently, the transfer function contains a positive power of \(z\), namely \(0.25z\), which corresponds to an advance.
parts.final: The system is FIR because \(h[n]=0.25\delta[n+1]+0.5\delta[n]+0.25\delta[n-1]\) has finite length. It is non-causal because \(h[-1]=0.25\neq 0\), i.e., the output depends on a future input sample.

parts.work:
The input is
\[
u[n]=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}n\right).
\]
For a real LTI system with frequency response \(H(\Omega)\), the response to \(\cos(\Omega_0 n)\) is
\[
y[n]=|H(\Omega_0)|\cos\left(\Omega_0 n+\angle H(\Omega_0)\right).
\]
Here \(\Omega_0=\pi/3\). From part (a),
\[
H(\Omega)=0.5(1+\cos\Omega).
\]
Therefore
\[
H\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=0.5\left(1+\cos\frac{\pi}{3}\right)
=0.5\left(1+\frac12\right)
=0.5\cdot\frac32
=\frac34.
\]
Since \(H(\pi/3)=3/4>0\), the phase is \(0\). Hence
\[
y[n]=\frac34\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}n\right).
\]

We are given a causal LTI system \(G\) with input
\[
u[n]=s[n]-s[n-2],
\]
where \(s[n]\) is the unit step. Thus
\[
u[0]=1,\quad u[1]=1,\quad u[n]=0 \text{ otherwise}.
\]
So \(u[n]=\delta[n]+\delta[n-1]\).

The output is
\[
y[n]=\delta[n-1]+\delta[n-4].
\]

For an LTI system,
\[
y[n]=u[n]*h[n].
\]
Since
\[
u[n]=\delta[n]+\delta[n-1],
\]
we have
\[
y[n]=h[n]+h[n-1].
\]
Therefore,
\[
h[n]+h[n-1]=\delta[n-1]+\delta[n-4].
\]

Because the system is causal, \(h[n]=0\) for \(n<0\). Now solve recursively.

For \(n<0\), \(h[n]=0\).

At \(n=0\):
\[
h[0]+h[-1]=\delta[-1]+\delta[-4]=0,
\]
so
\[
h[0]=0.
\]

At \(n=1\):
\[
h[1]+h[0]=\delta[0]+\delta[-3]=1,
\]
so
\[
h[1]=1.
\]

At \(n=2\):
\[
h[2]+h[1]=\delta[1]+\delta[-2]=0,
\]
so
\[
h[2]=-1.
\]

At \(n=3\):
\[
h[3]+h[2]=\delta[2]+\delta[-1]=0,
\]
so
\[
h[3]=1.
\]

At \(n=4\):
\[
h[4]+h[3]=\delta[3]+\delta[0]=1,
\]
so
\[
h[4]=0.
\]

At \(n=5\):
\[
h[5]+h[4]=\delta[4]+\delta[1]=0,
\]
so
\[
h[5]=0.
\]

For \(n>5\), the right-hand side is zero, and once two consecutive \(h\) values are zero, all later values remain zero. Hence
\[
h[n]=0 \quad \text{for } n\ge 5.
\]

Thus
\[
h[n]=\delta[n-1]-\delta[n-2]+\delta[n-3].
\]

Check:
\[
h[n]+h[n-1]
=(\delta[n-1]-\delta[n-2]+\delta[n-3])
+(\delta[n-2]-\delta[n-3]+\delta[n-4])
=\delta[n-1]+\delta[n-4],
\]
which matches \(y[n]\).

A causal LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if its impulse response is absolutely summable:
\[
\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|h[n]|<\infty.
\]
Here,
\[
h[n]=\delta[n-1]-\delta[n-2]+\delta[n-3],
\]
so
\[
\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|h[n]|=|1|+|-1|+|1|=3<\infty.
\]
Therefore, the system is BIBO stable.

For each signal \(x_i(t)=\cos(\omega_i t+\pi/4)\), one period has length \(T_i\), so the fundamental angular frequency is
\[
\omega_i=\frac{2\pi}{T_i}.
\]
We sample starting at \(t=0\) with sampling time \(T_{s_i}\). The number of samples in one period is
\[
N_i=\frac{T_i}{T_{s_i}},
\]
assuming this is an integer. The sampled sequence is
\[
x_i[n]=x_i(nT_{s_i})=\cos\left(\omega_i nT_{s_i}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{T_i}nT_{s_i}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N_i}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
\]
Using Euler’s formula,
\[
x_i[n]=\frac12 e^{j\pi/4}e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N_i}n}
+\frac12 e^{-j\pi/4}e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N_i}n}.
\]
The DFS convention is
\[
x[n]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]e^{jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}.
\]
Thus a term \(e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N}n}\) corresponds to \(X[1]=N\cdot \frac12 e^{j\pi/4}\), and a term \(e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}n}=e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N}(N-1)n}\) corresponds to \(X[N-1]=N\cdot \frac12 e^{-j\pi/4}\). All other DFS coefficients are zero.

(a) \(T_1=3,\ T_{s_1}=1\). Then
\[
N_1=\frac{3}{1}=3.
\]
So
\[
X_1[1]=\frac{3}{2}e^{j\pi/4},\qquad
X_1[2]=\frac{3}{2}e^{-j\pi/4},\qquad
X_1[0]=0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
X_1[k]=\frac{3}{2}e^{j\pi/4}\delta[(k-1)\bmod 3]
+\frac{3}{2}e^{-j\pi/4}\delta[(k-2)\bmod 3],
\quad k=0,1,2.
\]

(b) \(T_2=16,\ T_{s_2}=5\). Then
\[
N_2=\frac{16}{5},
\]
which is not an integer. Therefore the sampled sequence over one recorded period does not contain an integer number of samples. The problem statement says we record one period and then uniformly sample it; with \(T_2=16\) and \(T_{s_2}=5\), the samples in \([0,16)\) occur at \(t=0,5,10,15\), giving \(4\) samples, not \(16/5\). Thus the natural DFS length for the recorded samples is \(N_2=4\), but the sampled signal is not periodic with period \(4\) in general because the continuous-time period is not an integer multiple of the sampling time. Interpreting the DFS of the finite record of \(4\) samples:
\[
x_2[n]=\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{16}(5n)+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{8}n+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),\qquad n=0,1,2,3.
\]
Compute values:
\[
x_2[0]=\cos(\pi/4)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},
\]
\[
x_2[1]=\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{8}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{7\pi}{8}\right)=-\cos(\pi/8),
\]
\[
x_2[2]=\cos\left(\frac{10\pi}{8}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos(3\pi/2)=0,
\]
\[
x_2[3]=\cos\left(\frac{15\pi}{8}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{17\pi}{8}\right)
=\cos\left(2\pi+\frac{\pi}{8}\right)=\cos(\pi/8).
\]
For \(N=4\), the DFS is
\[
X_2[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{3}x_2[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{4}n}
=\sum_{n=0}^{3}x_2[n]e^{-jk\frac{\pi}{2}n}.
\]
Compute:
\[
X_2[0]=x_2[0]+x_2[1]+x_2[2]+x_2[3]
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-\cos(\pi/8)+0+\cos(\pi/8)
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
\[
X_2[1]=x_2[0]+x_2[1]e^{-j\pi/2}+x_2[2]e^{-j\pi}+x_2[3]e^{-j3\pi/2}.
\]
Since \(e^{-j\pi/2}=-j\), \(e^{-j\pi}=-1\), \(e^{-j3\pi/2}=j\),
\[
X_2[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-j(-\cos(\pi/8))+0+j\cos(\pi/8)
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+j\cos(\pi/8)+j\cos(\pi/8)
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+j2\cos(\pi/8).
\]
\[
X_2[2]=x_2[0]+x_2[1]e^{-j\pi}+x_2[2]e^{-j2\pi}+x_2[3]e^{-j3\pi}
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\cos(\pi/8)+0-\cos(\pi/8)
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
\[
X_2[3]=x_2[0]+x_2[1]e^{-j3\pi/2}+x_2[2]e^{-j3\pi}+x_2[3]e^{-j9\pi/2}.
\]
Here \(e^{-j3\pi/2}=j\), \(e^{-j3\pi}=-1\), \(e^{-j9\pi/2}=e^{-j\pi/2}=-j\). Thus
\[
X_2[3]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+j(-\cos(\pi/8))+0-j\cos(\pi/8)
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-j2\cos(\pi/8).
\]
So for the \(4\)-sample record,
\[
X_2[0]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\quad
X_2[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+j2\cos(\pi/8),\quad
X_2[2]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\quad
X_2[3]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-j2\cos(\pi/8).
\]
If instead one insists on using \(N=16/5\), that is not an integer and the DFS is not defined in the standard way. The standard interpretation is the finite record of \(4\) samples above.

(c) \(T_3=16,\ T_{s_3}=9\). Then
\[
N_3=\frac{16}{9},
\]
again not an integer. The samples in one period \([0,16)\) occur at \(t=0,9\), giving \(2\) samples. Thus take \(N_3=2\) for the finite record:
\[
x_3[n]=\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{16}(9n)+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{9\pi}{8}n+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),\qquad n=0,1.
\]
Compute:
\[
x_3[0]=\cos(\pi/4)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},
\]
\[
x_3[1]=\cos\left(\frac{9\pi}{8}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{11\pi}{8}\right)
=\cos\left(\pi+\frac{3\pi}{8}\right)
=-\cos(3\pi/8).
\]
For \(N=2\),
\[
X_3[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{1}x_3[n]e^{-jk\pi n}.
\]
Thus
\[
X_3[0]=x_3[0]+x_3[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-\cos(3\pi/8),
\]
\[
X_3[1]=x_3[0]-x_3[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\cos(3\pi/8).
\]
So
\[
X_3[0]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-\cos(3\pi/8),\qquad
X_3[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\cos(3\pi/8).
\]
parts.final:
(a) For \(T_1=3,\ T_{s_1}=1\), \(N_1=3\):
\[
X_1[0]=0,\qquad
X_1[1]=\frac{3}{2}e^{j\pi/4},\qquad
X_1[2]=\frac{3}{2}e^{-j\pi/4}.
\]

(b) For \(T_2=16,\ T_{s_2}=5\), the samples in one period are at \(t=0,5,10,15\), so the finite record has \(N_2=4\):
\[
X_2[0]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\quad
X_2[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+j2\cos(\pi/8),\quad
X_2[2]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\quad
X_2[3]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-j2\cos(\pi/8).
\]
(Using \(N=16/5\) is not valid since it is not an integer.)

(c) For \(T_3=16,\ T_{s_3}=9\), the samples in one period are at \(t=0,9\), so the finite record has \(N_3=2\):
\[
X_3[0]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-\cos(3\pi/8),\qquad
X_3[1]=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\cos(3\pi/8).
\]

parts.work:
Aliasing occurs when the sampling rate is not greater than twice the highest frequency present in the signal. For a real cosine at frequency \(f_i=\omega_i/(2\pi)=1/T_i\), the Nyquist condition is
\[
f_{s_i}=\frac1{T_{s_i}}>2f_i=\frac{2}{T_i}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
T_{s_i}<\frac{T_i}{2}.
\]

(a) \(T_1=3,\ T_{s_1}=1\). Here
\[
\frac{T_1}{2}=1.5,\qquad T_{s_1}=1<1.5.
\]
So the sampling rate is above Nyquist; no aliasing occurs.

(b) \(T_2=16,\ T_{s_2}=5\). Here
\[
\frac{T_2}{2}=8,\qquad T_{s_2}=5<8.
\]
So the sampling rate is above Nyquist; no aliasing occurs.

(c) \(T_3=16,\ T_{s_3}=9\). Here
\[
\frac{T_3}{2}=8,\qquad T_{s_3}=9>8.
\]
So the sampling rate is below Nyquist; aliasing occurs.

Equivalently, in terms of normalized frequency, the sampled cosine has digital frequency \(\Omega_i=2\pi T_{s_i}/T_i\). Aliasing occurs if this exceeds \(\pi\) modulo \(2\pi\) in a way that folds to a different frequency. For (c), \(\Omega_3=2\pi(9/16)=9\pi/8>\pi\), so the frequency folds to \(2\pi-9\pi/8=7\pi/8\), which is different from \(9\pi/8\); hence aliasing occurs. For (a), \(\Omega_1=2\pi/3<\pi\); for (b), \(\Omega_2=2\pi(5/16)=5\pi/8<\pi\). Thus only (c) aliases.
parts.final:
(a) No aliasing, since \(T_{s_1}=1<T_1/2=1.5\).

(b) No aliasing, since \(T_{s_2}=5<T_2/2=8\).

(c) Aliasing occurs, since \(T_{s_3}=9>T_3/2=8\).

parts.work:
The system is
\[
y[n]=0.5\,y[n-2]+u[n]-u[n-2].
\]
The input is periodic with period \(N=4\):
\[
u[n]=1+0.5\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right)+0.25\cos(\pi n).
\]
We use the DFS convention
\[
x[n]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]e^{jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n},
\]
so for \(N=4\),
\[
x[n]=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}X[k]e^{jk\frac{\pi}{2}n}.
\]

First find the DFS coefficients \(U[k]\) of \(u[n]\). Write each term in complex exponential form.

The constant term:
\[
1 \longleftrightarrow U[0]\text{ contribution }=4.
\]

The sine term:
\[
0.5\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right)
=0.5\cdot \frac{e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}n}-e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}n}}{2j}
=\frac{1}{4j}e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}n}-\frac{1}{4j}e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}n}.
\]
Since \(e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}n}=e^{j\frac{3\pi}{2}n}\) for period \(4\), this contributes
\[
U[1]=\frac{4}{4j}=\frac1j=-j,
\qquad
U[3]=-\frac{4}{4j}=-\frac1j=j.
\]

The cosine term:
\[
0.25\cos(\pi n)
=0.25\cdot \frac{e^{j\pi n}+e^{-j\pi n}}2
=\frac18 e^{j\pi n}+\frac18 e^{-j\pi n}.
\]
Since \(e^{j\pi n}=e^{j\frac{2\pi}{4}2n}\), this contributes to \(k=2\):
\[
U[2]=\frac{4}{8}+\frac{4}{8}=1.
\]

Thus
\[
U[0]=4,\qquad U[1]=-j,\qquad U[2]=1,\qquad U[3]=j.
\]

Now apply the difference equation in the DFS domain. Because the system is LTI and the input is periodic, each exponential \(e^{jk(2\pi/N)n}\) is an eigenfunction. For a component \(e^{jk(2\pi/N)n}\), the output component is multiplied by
\[
H(e^{j\omega_k})=\frac{1-e^{-j2\omega_k}}{1-0.5e^{-j2\omega_k}},
\qquad \omega_k=k\frac{2\pi}{N}=k\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
Equivalently, from
\[
y[n]-0.5y[n-2]=u[n]-u[n-2],
\]
taking DFS gives
\[
Y[k]\left(1-0.5e^{-j2\omega_k}\right)
=U[k]\left(1-e^{-j2\omega_k}\right),
\]
so
\[
Y[k]=U[k]\frac{1-e^{-j2\omega_k}}{1-0.5e^{-j2\omega_k}}.
\]

Compute for each \(k=0,1,2,3\).

For \(k=0\), \(\omega_0=0\):
\[
e^{-j2\omega_0}=1,
\]
so
\[
\frac{1-1}{1-0.5}=0.
\]
Hence
\[
Y[0]=0.
\]

For \(k=1\), \(\omega_1=\frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(2\omega_1=\pi\):
\[
e^{-j2\omega_1}=e^{-j\pi}=-1.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{1-(-1)}{1-0.5(-1)}
=\frac{2}{1+0.5}
=\frac{2}{1.5}
=\frac43.
\]
Therefore
\[
Y[1]=U[1]\cdot \frac43
=(-j)\frac43
=-\frac{4}{3}j.
\]

For \(k=2\), \(\omega_2=\pi\), so \(2\omega_2=2\pi\):
\[
e^{-j2\omega_2}=e^{-j2\pi}=1.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{1-1}{1-0.5}=0,
\]
so
\[
Y[2]=0.
\]

For \(k=3\), \(\omega_3=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), so \(2\omega_3=3\pi\):
\[
e^{-j2\omega_3}=e^{-j3\pi}=-1.
\]
Thus the multiplier is again
\[
\frac{1-(-1)}{1-0.5(-1)}=\frac43.
\]
Therefore
\[
Y[3]=U[3]\cdot \frac43
=j\frac43
=\frac{4}{3}j.
\]

Hence the DFS coefficients of \(y[n]\) are
\[
Y[0]=0,\qquad
Y[1]=-\frac{4}{3}j,\qquad
Y[2]=0,\qquad
Y[3]=\frac{4}{3}j.
\]

As a check, reconstruct:
\[
y[n]=\frac14\left(-\frac{4}{3}j e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}n}+\frac{4}{3}j e^{j\frac{3\pi}{2}n}\right)
=\frac13\left(-j e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}n}+j e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}n}\right)
=\frac13\cdot 2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right)
=\frac23\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}n\right).
\]
Indeed, the constant and \(\cos(\pi n)\) terms are annihilated by the system because they are at frequencies where \(1-e^{-j2\omega}=0\), while the sine term is scaled by \(4/3\).

We are given the DFT definition
\[
X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}, \qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.
\]
The vector \(b\in\mathbb{C}^N\) collects the DFT coefficients, so \(b_k=X[k]\). The vector \(y\in\mathbb{C}^N\) collects the time-domain sequence, so \(y_n=x[n]\). We want \(y=\Phi b\), i.e.
\[
y_i=\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}[\Phi]_{il}\,b_l, \qquad i=0,\ldots,N-1.
\]
Since \(b_l=X[l]\), we need
\[
x[i]=\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}[\Phi]_{il}X[l].
\]
The inverse DFT relation is
\[
x[n]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]e^{jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}.
\]
Setting \(n=i\) and using summation index \(l\) instead of \(k\),
\[
x[i]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}X[l]e^{jl\frac{2\pi}{N}i}.
\]
Comparing with
\[
x[i]=\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}[\Phi]_{il}X[l],
\]
we identify
\[
[\Phi]_{il}=\frac{1}{N}e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N}il}, \qquad i=0,\ldots,N-1,\quad l=0,\ldots,N-1.
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) is the inverse DFT matrix (up to the conventional \(1/N\) normalization), and \(y=\Phi b\) reconstructs the time sequence from all DFT coefficients.
parts.final:
\[
[\Phi]_{il}=\frac{1}{N}e^{j\frac{2\pi}{N}il},\qquad i,l=0,\ldots,N-1.
\]
Equivalently, \(\Phi=\frac{1}{N}W^{*}\), where \(W_{kn}=e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}kn}\) is the DFT matrix.

parts.work:
We must show that the DFT relation is linear, i.e. that the mapping from the time-domain vector \(y\) to the DFT vector \(b\) (and equivalently the reconstruction \(y=\Phi b\)) is linear.

Let \(x[n]\) and \(z[n]\) be two length-\(N\) sequences with DFT coefficients \(X[k]\) and \(Z[k]\), respectively. Let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C}\). Define
\[
w[n]=\alpha x[n]+\beta z[n].
\]
Its DFT is, by definition,
\[
W[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}w[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}
=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\alpha x[n]+\beta z[n]\bigr)e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}.
\]
Using linearity of finite sums,
\[
W[k]=\alpha\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}
+\beta\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}z[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}
=\alpha X[k]+\beta Z[k].
\]
Hence the DFT operator is linear.

Equivalently, in matrix form, the DFT relation is \(b=Wy\) with \(W_{kn}=e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}kn}\). Since matrix multiplication is linear,
\[
W(\alpha y+\beta z)=\alpha Wy+\beta Wz,
\]
so \(b\) depends linearly on \(y\). The reconstruction map \(y=\Phi b\) is also linear because \(\Phi\) is a fixed matrix:
\[
\Phi(\alpha b_1+\beta b_2)=\alpha\Phi b_1+\beta\Phi b_2.
\]
Therefore the DFT relation and the reconstruction both satisfy linearity (superposition).
parts.final:
For any sequences \(x[n],z[n]\) with DFTs \(X[k],Z[k]\) and any scalars \(\alpha,\beta\),
\[
\mathrm{DFT}\{\alpha x[n]+\beta z[n]\}=\alpha X[k]+\beta Z[k].
\]
Equivalently, \(b=Wy\) and \(y=\Phi b\) are linear maps because \(W\) and \(\Phi\) are fixed matrices. Thus linearity (superposition) holds.
